The radar absorbing structure composite (RAS) studied contains a circuit analogue structure (CAS) made from conductive aluminum foil.
CAS acts as a reflection screen causing interference between incident and reflected electromagnetic waves.
Introduction of CAS improves radar absorption by 3 to 5 dB in the 8–18 GHz frequency range compared to RAS without CAS.
Increasing CAS size shifts the maximum absorption peak to lower frequencies.
Increasing the electromagnetic parameters of the medium ply shifts the absorption peak to lower frequencies.
Increasing the thickness of the medium laminate shifts the absorption peak to lower frequencies.
Materials used include epoxy resin, glass fiber SW-220, carbon fiber T300, absorbent iron powder, carbon black, and aluminum foil (0.03 mm).
CAS impedance is modeled with a formula involving geometric parameters and foil conductance.
Reflectivity of RAS with CAS is calculated using transmission line theory treating CAS as parallel resistance.
The fundamental requirements for RAS are maximum absorption, minimum reflection, and broad absorption bandwidth.
Minimum reflection requires gradual impedance transition from weakly to strongly absorbing media, which can increase RAS thickness.
Measurements of complex permittivity and permeability were done using a network analyzer per GJB 2038-94.
Reflection measurements were also conducted according to GJB 2038-94 standards.
CAS provides flexibility in design by enabling smooth or stepped impedance changes.
The aluminum foil used for CAS is 0.03 mm thick.
The composite specimens were prepared by layering prepregs and integrating CAS as a foil layer.
The maximum input resistance of RAS containing CAS moves to lower frequency with increasing CAS size, electromagnetic parameters, or thickness.
CAS can be considered equivalent to a parallel resistance in a transmission line model.
The study references earlier work on radar cross-section reduction and circuit analogue absorbers.
The RAS thicknesses studied included 4 mm and 4.5 mm in various experiments.
